components/c05.title: Rate Limiting visual walkthrough
components/c05.summary: Start with placement and ownership, then trace one atomic token-bucket decision, and finish with the coordination and failure choices introduced by a distributed gateway fleet.

items.title: Where rate limiting lives
items.purpose: Identify the enforcement point, policy source, counter state, response contract, and protected downstream service.
items.description: The edge authenticates enough of the request to select a key such as user, API key, tenant, or IP. A limiter applies versioned policy and performs an atomic state update before the request reaches scarce downstream capacity.

flow.title: Identify
flow.detail: Derive the limit key and endpoint or resource class after trusted authentication.

flow.title: Load policy
flow.detail: Resolve capacity, refill rate, request cost, exemptions, and policy version.

flow.title: Spend atomically
flow.detail: Update token or counter state without a read-modify-write race.

flow.title: Allow or reject
flow.detail: Forward allowed work; otherwise return 429 with Retry-After and rate-limit headers.

flow.title: Observe
flow.detail: Record decisions, saturation, hot keys, store latency, and fail-open or fail-closed events.

numbers.label: Example capacity
numbers.detail: Maximum immediate burst.

numbers.label: Example refill
numbers.detail: Sustained admitted rate.

numbers.label: Reject response
numbers.detail: Include Retry-After when calculable.

tradeoffs: Edge enforcement is cheap and early but may lack application context.
Service-level limits are precise but allow rejected work deeper into the stack.

items.title: One atomic token-bucket decision
items.purpose: Trace refill, spend, allow, and Retry-After calculation as one race-free state transition.
items.description: The stored state is tokens plus the last refill timestamp. One atomic script computes elapsed refill, caps the bucket at capacity, spends the request cost when possible, and returns the remaining budget and reset estimate.

flow.title: Read inputs
flow.detail: Use key, capacity B, refill rate r, cost c, and a monotonic server-side time source.

flow.title: Refill
flow.detail: tokens = min(B, tokens + r × elapsed).

flow.title: Decide
flow.detail: If tokens ≥ c, subtract c and allow; otherwise preserve state and reject.

flow.title: Explain
flow.detail: Return remaining tokens and Retry-After = ceil((c − tokens) ÷ r).

flow.title: Expire idle keys
flow.detail: Set a TTL long enough for a full refill so inactive identities do not consume memory forever.

numbers.label: Burst
numbers.detail: An idle client can spend accumulated tokens immediately.

numbers.label: Long-run rate
numbers.detail: Refill limits sustained traffic.

numbers.label: State
numbers.detail: Tokens and last-refill time.

tradeoffs: Token bucket permits controlled bursts; leaky bucket instead smooths output.
Exact sliding logs remove approximation but store one timestamp per request.

items.title: Distributed counters, reservations, and failure policy
items.purpose: Show why local counters overshoot a global quota and where accuracy can be traded for latency and availability.
items.description: Twenty independent gateways each enforcing the full quota can admit roughly twenty times the intended traffic. Shared atomic state fixes accuracy but adds a network hop. Local token reservations amortize that hop while accepting bounded overshoot.

flow.title: Shard by limit key
flow.detail: Consistent hashing spreads users while keeping each user's state on one counter shard.

flow.title: Execute atomically
flow.detail: A Redis script or transactional primitive owns refill and spend for that key.

flow.title: Reserve locally when needed
flow.detail: Gateways lease small token batches to remove a shared-store round trip from every request.

flow.title: Bound the error
flow.detail: Reservation size × active gateways defines the worst-case overshoot.

flow.title: Choose failure semantics
flow.detail: Fail closed for billing or security; fail open or use an emergency local limit for low-risk availability paths.

numbers.label: Gateway fleet
numbers.detail: Local full quotas could admit ≈20×.

numbers.label: Shared check
numbers.detail: Accuracy costs coordination latency.

numbers.label: Reservation error
numbers.detail: Make the accuracy budget explicit.

tradeoffs: Shared counters are accurate but add latency and a dependency to every request.
Sticky routing is fast but imbalances hot clients and complicates failover.

ddia/ch05.title: Replication visual walkthrough
ddia/ch05.summary: Replication needs four sheets because the topologies solve different problems. Compare them first, then study single-leader lag and failover, multi-leader conflict handling, and leaderless quorum repair independently.

items.title: Single-leader, multi-leader, and leaderless
items.purpose: Choose a topology by locating write authority, replication direction, conflict surface, and failure behavior.
items.description: Single-leader centralizes write order; multi-leader accepts local writes in several locations and must merge conflicts; leaderless sends each operation to multiple replicas and reconciles versions. No topology provides latency, availability, and simple consistency simultaneously.

flow.title: Locate write authority
flow.detail: One leader, several leaders, or any replica determines the coordination model.

flow.title: Trace propagation
flow.detail: Identify synchronous acknowledgements, asynchronous logs, and cross-region links.

flow.title: Find concurrency
flow.detail: More than one write authority means concurrent versions must be detected and resolved.

flow.title: Test a partition
flow.detail: Ask which side accepts writes, what the client observes, and what must reconcile later.

numbers.label: Single leader
numbers.detail: Simple order; leader is a coordination point.

numbers.label: Multi-leader
numbers.detail: Local writes; conflict handling required.

numbers.label: Leaderless
numbers.detail: Tune read and write quorums.

tradeoffs: Centralized ordering simplifies correctness but adds write latency and failover complexity.
Multiple write authorities improve locality and availability but move complexity into conflict resolution.

items.title: Single-leader replication, lag, and failover
items.purpose: Trace one write through the leader and log, then connect acknowledgement timing to lag, stale reads, and data loss.
items.description: The leader assigns a single order and streams a replication log to followers. Synchronous followers improve durability but can block writes; asynchronous followers reduce latency but can lose acknowledged writes and serve stale reads after a leader failure.

flow.title: Write the leader
flow.detail: The client sends all mutations to the elected leader.

flow.title: Append and apply
flow.detail: The leader records the write and applies it in log order.

flow.title: Replicate
flow.detail: Followers consume the log synchronously or asynchronously and expose a replay position.

flow.title: Acknowledge
flow.detail: The durability contract depends on which follower acknowledgements are required before success.

flow.title: Serve reads safely
flow.detail: Use leader pinning or log-position checks for read-your-writes and monotonic reads.

flow.title: Fail over
flow.detail: Detect failure, elect the most caught-up follower, fence the old leader, and reconfigure clients.

numbers.label: Sync follower
numbers.detail: Balances durability and availability.

numbers.label: Lag
numbers.detail: Track bytes, entries, and seconds behind.

numbers.label: RPO
numbers.detail: Recent acknowledged writes may be lost.

tradeoffs: Synchronous replication improves freshness and durability but blocks on slow or failed replicas.
Aggressive failover reduces outage time but increases false elections and split-brain risk.

items.title: Multi-leader replication and conflict resolution
items.purpose: Show how local writes become concurrent and why detection, deterministic merge, and convergence are part of the write model.
items.description: Each region accepts writes locally and exchanges them asynchronously. When two leaders update the same object without observing each other, the system must preserve causal metadata, detect concurrency, and apply a deterministic policy such as an application merge or CRDT.

flow.title: Write locally
flow.detail: Region A and Region B acknowledge nearby clients without a cross-ocean round trip.

flow.title: Replicate asynchronously
flow.detail: Each leader sends operations and causal metadata to the other leaders.

flow.title: Detect concurrency
flow.detail: Version vectors distinguish overwrites from genuinely concurrent updates.

flow.title: Resolve deliberately
flow.detail: Prefer application merge or CRDT semantics; last-write-wins silently discards data.

flow.title: Converge
flow.detail: Replicate the resolved version until every leader and follower agrees.

numbers.label: Regions
numbers.detail: Every added authority expands the conflict surface.

numbers.label: Local write
numbers.detail: Avoids cross-region acknowledgement latency.

numbers.label: Conflict window
numbers.detail: Longer lag permits more concurrency.

tradeoffs: Home-region routing avoids most conflicts but sacrifices local writes during that region's outage.
Last-write-wins is operationally simple but converts concurrency into silent data loss.

items.title: Leaderless quorums, repair, and hinted handoff
items.purpose: Trace writes and reads across replicas, then separate overlap math from the background mechanisms that actually converge stale copies.
items.description: A coordinator sends writes to n replicas and succeeds after w acknowledgements; reads query r replicas and reconcile returned versions. When w + r > n the sets overlap, but sloppy quorums, partial writes, and concurrency mean this is not automatically linearizable.

flow.title: Write n replicas
flow.detail: The coordinator sends a versioned value to the replica set.

flow.title: Wait for w
flow.detail: Return success when the configured write quorum acknowledges.

flow.title: Read r
flow.detail: Fetch multiple versions, compare clocks, and return or merge the newest causal value.

flow.title: Repair
flow.detail: Read repair updates stale replicas encountered by traffic; anti-entropy handles cold data in the background.

flow.title: Survive unavailable homes
flow.detail: Sloppy quorum stores a hint on reachable nodes and hands it back to the intended replica later.

numbers.label: Example
numbers.detail: Read and write sets must overlap.

numbers.label: Overlap
numbers.detail: Necessary for quorum freshness, not sufficient for linearizability.

numbers.label: Fast-read option
numbers.detail: Cheap reads; writes lose availability if one replica is down.

tradeoffs: Larger w improves read freshness but reduces write availability.
Sloppy quorums keep writes available during partitions but weaken immediate read-your-write behavior on home replicas.

design-problems/p01.title: URL Shortener visual walkthrough
design-problems/p01.summary: Study the system map first, then trace creation and redirection independently. The GET sheet keeps cache hit, cache miss, and not-found behavior together because those branches share one serving path.

items.title: Architecture, priorities, and boundaries
items.purpose: Place every service, store, cache, and asynchronous boundary before walking either API.
items.description: The mapping store is authoritative, Redis accelerates the read-heavy redirect path, and click analytics leaves the request path through a durable queue. Creation may coordinate for uniqueness; redirection is optimized for latency and availability.

flow.title: Create
flow.detail: The authenticated client submits a long URL through the edge to the stateless URL service.

flow.title: Generate and persist
flow.detail: Allocate a unique ID, encode it in Base62, and durably store code → URL before responding.

flow.title: Redirect
flow.detail: Resolve GET /{code} from Redis when possible and fall back to a point read from the mapping store.

flow.title: Measure asynchronously
flow.detail: Publish click events to a queue so analytics workers and the warehouse cannot delay redirects.

numbers.detail: Engineer the redirect path first.

numbers.label: Redirects

numbers.detail: Seven characters cover the five-year estimate.

Sequential IDs avoid collisions but expose traffic volume; random IDs hide volume but require collision retries.

items.title: Create a short URL
items.purpose: Trace the write path, including validation, idempotency, unique-code allocation, persistence, and cache warming.
items.description: Creation is the correctness path. A retry must return the same mapping rather than create another code, and the service must never acknowledge a code before its mapping is durable. ID ranges remove per-request coordination from a globally unique counter.

flow.title: Authenticate and limit
flow.detail: Protect the public create endpoint from spam and expensive abuse.

flow.title: Validate and normalize
flow.detail: Check scheme, length, denylist, optional alias, and expiry without rewriting URL semantics.

flow.title: Deduplicate retries
flow.detail: Bind the client idempotency key to the eventual response.

flow.title: Allocate and encode
flow.detail: Claim an ID from a preallocated range and encode it in Base62; custom aliases use a uniqueness check.

flow.title: Persist
flow.detail: Conditionally insert code → long URL into the source-of-truth mapping store.

flow.title: Warm and respond
flow.detail: Populate Redis after the durable write and return the short URL.

numbers.label: Average writes
numbers.detail: 100M creates ÷ 86,400 seconds.

numbers.label: Peak target
numbers.detail: Budget roughly 2–3× average.

numbers.label: Five-year rows
numbers.detail: About 90 TB at 500 bytes per mapping.

tradeoffs: Preallocated counter ranges are collision-free and fast, but codes remain enumerable.
Synchronous cache warming improves the first read but should not make a successful durable write fail.

items.title: Redirect: cache hit, miss, and not found
items.purpose: Keep the serving path and its three outcomes on one sheet so the latency and availability decisions are easy to compare.
items.description: The redirect endpoint is public, read-heavy, and availability-critical. A hit returns immediately; a miss performs one primary-key read and backfills Redis; an absent or expired mapping is negative-cached briefly. Click events are emitted after resolution and never block the response.

flow.title: Route
flow.detail: The edge validates the code shape, applies abuse controls, and routes to a nearby stateless redirect service.

flow.title: Cache hit
flow.detail: Redis returns the long URL; issue 301 or 302 immediately and emit a click event asynchronously.

flow.title: Cache miss
flow.detail: Point-read the mapping store, check expiry, backfill Redis with TTL jitter, and redirect.

flow.title: Not found
flow.detail: Negative-cache the miss briefly to absorb repeated scans, then return 404.

flow.title: Degrade deliberately
flow.detail: If the store is unavailable, continue serving cached mappings; buffer or drop analytics before delaying redirects.

numbers.label: Average reads
numbers.detail: 10B redirects per day.

numbers.label: Peak reads
numbers.detail: Edge and cache capacity dominate.

numbers.label: Latency focus
numbers.detail: Target the warm regional path, not global origin latency.

tradeoffs: Long cache TTLs lower cost and latency but delay deletion or destination changes.
Negative caching protects the store from scans but can briefly hide a newly created code.
